A Generalised Framework for Property-Driven Machine Learning

Thomas Flinkow Affiliation: Maynooth University, Maynooth, Ireland E-mail {thomas.flinkow,rosemary.monahan}@mu.ie    Marco Casadio Affiliation: Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, UK E-mail {mc248,ck2049}@hw.ac.uk    Colin Kessler Affiliation: Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, UK E-mail {mc248,ck2049}@hw.ac.uk Affiliation: University of Edinburgh and Edinburgh Centre for Robotics, Edinburgh, UK    Rosemary Monahan Affiliation: Maynooth University, Maynooth, Ireland E-mail {thomas.flinkow,rosemary.monahan}@mu.ie    Ekaterina Komendantskaya Affiliation: Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, UK E-mail {mc248,ck2049}@hw.ac.uk Affiliation: University of Southampton, Southampton, UK E-mail e.komendantskaya@soton.ac.uk
Abstract

Neural networks have been shown to frequently fail to satisfy critical safety and correctness properties after training, highlighting the pressing need for training methods that incorporate such properties directly. While adversarial training can be used to improve robustness to small perturbations within ϵ\epsilon-cubes, domains other than computer vision—such as control systems and natural language processing—may require more flexible input region specifications via generalised hyper-rectangles. Meanwhile, differentiable logics offer a way to encode arbitrary logical constraints as additional loss terms that guide the learning process towards satisfying these constraints. In this paper, we investigate how these two complementary approaches can be unified within a single framework for property-driven machine learning. We show that well-known properties from the literature are subcases of this general approach, and we demonstrate its practical effectiveness on a case study involving a neural network controller for a drone system. Our framework is publicly available at https://github.com/tflinkow/property-driven-ml.

Keywords:
Machine Learning Adversarial Training Property-driven Training Neuro-symbolic AI Differentiable Logics

1 Introduction

Neural networks have been shown to frequently fail to satisfy properties of interest after training [31, 11], and even the most accurate networks are known to be susceptible to adversarial attacks, i.e. inputs that resemble the training data but fall outside of the learnt distribution [53, 26]. This puts restrictions on their use in safety-critical domains. To address this gap, numerous formal verification tools11 1 For an overview of the state-of-the art in formal verification of neural networks, we refer the interested reader to [28, 56, 39, 3]. have been proposed in the past few years, including Marabou [31, 32, 63], Branch-and-Bound [8], NNV [54, 40], and α,β\alpha,\beta-CROWN [67, 64, 65, 60, 66, 51] (winner of the recent Neural Network Verification Competitions (VNN-COMP) [4, 47, 6, 7]).

Crucially, the success of the verification tools depends on obtaining models that actually yield the desired verification properties after training. However, neural networks obtained via standard training with gradient descent tend to fail verification properties of interest, which is why there is a need for training methods that combine data-driven with property-driven training.

Standard optimisation methods that improve robustness.

In the simplest case, data augmentation and adversarial training [26, 42] can be used to improve neural network robustness. Data augmentation artificially enlarges the data set (e.g. by adding noise, or applying rotation, translation, scaling, etc.). Adversarial training aims to find the worst-case perturbation within ϵ\epsilon-distance around an input and integrates the loss computed for the perturbations into the training process. As an example, consider a property frequently used in image classification: ϵ,δ\epsilon,\delta-robustness (or local robustness) of a neural network ff, expressed as ∀x→.∥x→0−x→∥≤ϵ⟶∥f⁡(x→0)−f⁡(x→)∥≤δ\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\lVert\vec{x}_{0}-\vec{x}\rVert\leq\epsilon\ \longrightarrow\ \lVert f(\vec{x}_{0})-f(\vec{x})\rVert\leq\delta, given an image x→0\vec{x}_{0} in the data set. Adversarial training (e.g. via Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM [26]) or Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) [42] algorithms) finds the perturbation in the ϵ\epsilon-vicinity of x→0\vec{x}_{0} for which the property ∥f⁡(x→0)−f⁡(x→)∥≤δ\lVert f(\vec{x}_{0})-f(\vec{x})\rVert\leq\delta fails and optimises the neural network towards correct classification of that sample.

Although these standard optimisation methods generally work well for computer vision models, they fail to generalise beyond this domain. In many scenarios outside of computer vision, we encounter properties in the form ∀x→.𝒫⁡(x→)⟶𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})), where preconditions 𝒫\mathcal{P} and postconditions 𝒬\mathcal{Q} differ substantially from the concrete instances used in the algorithms that optimise networks for ϵ,δ\epsilon,\delta-robustness. Firstly, the properties 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} do not have to be local, i.e. do not have to relate to given data points. Global properties of the input space can constrain input vectors in arbitrary ways. Secondly, 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} do not have to be atomic, and can be given by arbitrary logical formulas.

In the last couple of years, several methods have been proposed in order to generalise adversarial training to optimisation tasks involving global properties and non-atomic properties.

Global properties and hyper-rectangles.

Generally, for a neural network f:ℝm→ℝnf\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, a global property 𝒫\mathcal{P} on the input space ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} is given by a number of constraints of the form li≤xi≤uil_{i}\leq x_{i}\leq u_{i}, for constants lil_{i}, uiu_{i}, and x→=[x1,…,xm]∈ℝm\vec{x}=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]\in\mathbb{R}^{m} being an element of the input space. As noticed by [9, 10, 24], such constraints generally give rise to the notion of a hyper-rectangle (described in more detail in Section 2.1), which generalises the notion of ϵ\epsilon-cubes frequently deployed in adversarial training.

Although initially investigated in the context of classifiers for large language models [9, 10] and for security applications [24], there is an even more common application domain for such properties: neural networks deployed in cyber-physical systems as neural controllers. The seminal neural network verification benchmark ACAS Xu22 2 The experimental neural network compression [29] of the unmanned variant ACAS Xu of the Airbourne Collision Avoidance System X (ACAS X) [35, 34]., for example, is defined via ten global properties that constrain sensor readings based on their intended semantics such as velocity, distance and angle to the intruder. Many neural network controllers yield similar verification conditions [43].

Non-atomic postconditions and differentiable logics.

Important examples where the postcondition 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is non-atomic have also been flagged in the literature [50, 21]. Often, constraints on the output should not just encourage the network to make the correct class prediction, but rather encode complex, expressive constraints on the outputs: for example, in DL2 [22], a constraint for CIFAR-100 [36] that refers to the probability of a group of people (consisting of the individual probabilities of the classes for baby, boy, girl, man, and woman) can be used to make misclassifications less severe; the network can be taught to make it more preferable to misclassify a man as a boy rather than as a bicycle.

It was suggested that differentiable logics (described in more detail in Section 2.2) can be used to translate arbitrary logical constraints into additional loss terms for optimisation. These loss terms generalise the loss ∥f⁡(x→0)−f⁡(x→)∥≤δ\lVert f(\vec{x}_{0})-f(\vec{x})\rVert\leq\delta used in the PGD or FGSM optimisation algorithms to a function that encodes an arbitrary property 𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})). This line of research was explored in [22, 57, 23].

Contributions.

This paper presents a generalised methodology for property-driven machine learning, combining the two existing lines of research into training with hyper-rectangles and differentiable logics. The result is a method that optimises arbitrary neural networks to arbitrary properties ∀x→.𝒫⁡(x→)⟶𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})) written in a subset of first-order logic. In particular, 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) and 𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})) can be expressed by arbitrary quantifier-free first-order formulae, such that occurrences of the neural network ff is permitted in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} but not in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is limited to constraints that have constant upper and lower bounds for each dimension.

We argue that this class of generalised properties is characteristic of properties deployed in verification of neural network controllers used in cyber-physical systems. This happens for two reasons:

  • •

    neural network controller modelling often comes with well-defined global constraints concerning input regions. These are usually given as assumptions on safe and unsafe sensor readings that, unlike pixels in images, have well-defined mathematical or physical meaning. This can give rise to a non-trivial property 𝒫\mathcal{P} expressed as a complex Boolean formula;

  • •

    a degree of freedom in the behaviour of a neural network controller is expected: i.e. we do not want to firmly prescribe the controller in every scenario (as this would diminish it to a classical controller), but want to only constrain unsafe actions. For example, in the ACAS Xu case, the property 𝒫\mathcal{P} “the distance to intruder is dangerously small” does not mandate “advise ‘strong left”’, but is rather expressed as “do not advise ‘clear of conflict”’, which boils down to a disjunctive prescription for 𝒬\mathcal{Q}: “weak or strong left or weak or strong right”. Generally, such verification scenarios result in non-trivial 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

We deploy a new case-study of a neural network controller (see [33] for more details) and use it to test our method. This use case gives us more flexibility in both property specification and training (as the ACAS Xu data set is not publicly released), but also presents a generalisation of the ACAS Xu case to regression models.

Paper outline.

In the following, we will first set the context of this work, explaining the theory and gaps of input region specification in Section 2.1, and of differentiable logics in Section 2.2, respectively. We describe our unifying framework combining (1) flexible input region specification via hyper-rectangles and (2) differentiable logics for translating arbitrary logical constraints into additional loss terms in Section 3 and show how well-known properties from the literature emerge as special cases of this framework. We briefly describe our Python implementation, publicly available at https://github.com/tflinkow/property-driven-ml. We show the effectiveness of this approach on MNIST and a case study involving a neural network controller for a glider drone in Section 4. Lastly, we conclude with a discussion, including limitations and possible areas of future work, in Section 5.

2 Context

2.1 Input Region Specification

As noted in [10], verification of neural networks has focused primarily on robustness verification, which requires a classification network f:ℝm→ℝnf\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} to assign the same class label for each element in each subspace 𝒮i⊆ℝm\mathcal{S}_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}. For computer vision tasks, these subspaces often take the shape of ϵ\epsilon-balls around all input vectors in the dataset. Formally, given an input x→\vec{x} and distance function ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert, the ϵ\epsilon-ball around x→\vec{x} of radius ϵ\epsilon is defined as:

𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ):={x→′∈ℝm:∥x→−x→′∥≤ϵ}\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon):=\{\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}:\lVert\vec{x}-\vec{x}^{\prime}\rVert\leq\epsilon\} (1)

In practice, it is common to use the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm [26], in which case these ϵ\epsilon-balls are also called ϵ\epsilon-cubes.

While ϵ\epsilon-bounded perturbations work reasonably well for computer vision tasks [61, 27], they are not necessarily as well suited for other tasks, such as natural language processing or low-dimensional problems (e.g. neural network controllers). In computer vision, images are seen as vectors in a continuous space and thus every point in that space corresponds to a valid image. In contrast, natural language processing input spaces are usually discrete, and ϵ\epsilon-balls around one sentence embedding may not in fact contain any other valid sentences [10].

Although the idea of generalising ϵ\epsilon-cubes to arbitrary hyper-rectangles has existed for a while, Casadio et al. [10] were the first to argue that hyper-rectangles can systematically be used in verification and property-driven training of neural networks. A multi-dimensional rectangle (or hyper-rectangle), is a shape defined by lower and upper bounds for each dimension, i.e. l→,u→∈ℝm\vec{l},\vec{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that l→≤u→\vec{l}\leq\vec{u} (component-wise). The hyper-rectangle H⁡(l→,u→)H(\vec{l},\vec{u}) is then defined as

H(l→,u→):={x→∈ℝm∣li≤xi≤ui,for all 1≤i≤m}.H(\vec{l},\vec{u}):=\{\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\mid l_{i}\leq x_{i}\leq u_{i},\ \text{for all }1\leq i\leq m\}. (2)

As visualised in Fig. 1, hyper-rectangles allow the specification of ϵ\epsilon-cubes, as well as more flexible local regions, and they can also be used to specify global input regions (not relative to specific inputs). For examples of such properties see [24, 9].

2.2 Property-driven Training

Training for robustness.

In standard machine learning, for a model fθf_{\theta} parametrised by θ\theta, optimal parameters θ∗\theta^{*} are obtained by using gradient descent to minimise a loss ℒ\mathcal{L} that quantifies the difference between the network’s actual output fθ​(x→)f_{\theta}(\vec{x}) and the desired output y→\vec{y}, shown in Eq. 3:

θ∗=arg​minθ⁡𝔼(x→,y→)∼𝒟​[ℒ⁡(x→,y→,fθ)]\theta^{*}=\argmin\limits_{\theta}\expected\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\ \bigl[\mathcal{L}(\vec{x},\vec{y};f_{\theta})\bigr] (3)

Adversarial training via FGSM / PGD algorithms [26, 42] finds adversarial examples and integrates them into the training process. Formally, the minimisation objective changes from the one shown in Eq. 3 to the one shown in Eq. 4, where x→′\vec{x}^{\prime} is an adversarial example within the ϵ\epsilon-cube around a given input x→\vec{x}.

θ∗=arg​minθ⁡𝔼(x→,y→)∼𝒟​[maxx→′∈𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ)⁡ℒ⁡(x→′,y→,fθ)]\theta^{*}=\argmin\limits_{\theta}\expected\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\ \biggl[\max\limits_{\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon)}\mathcal{L}(\vec{x}^{\prime},\vec{y};f_{\theta})\biggr] (4)

Therefore, adversarial training consists of a two-step process: an inner maximisation problem to select the worst-case adversarial perturbation within the ϵ\epsilon-cube around a clean data point x→\vec{x}, followed by adapting the network weights to reduce the loss caused by this adversarial perturbation. Madry et al. [42] proposed to use PGD to approximately solve the inner optimisation problem.

Training to satisfy arbitrary logical constraints.

Adversarial training aims to improve prediction accuracy on perturbed inputs, i.e. similar inputs should be assigned the same class label. It has been shown in [11] that training for one kind of robustness does not necessarily imply another; for example, while adversarial training improves standard robustness (i.e. given an input x→0\vec{x}_{0}, standard robustness requires ∀x→∈𝔹⁡(x→0,ϵ).∥f⁡(x→0)−f⁡(x→)∥≤δ\forall\vec{x}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x}_{0};\epsilon)\ldotp\lVert f(\vec{x}_{0})-f(\vec{x})\rVert\leq\delta), most works on verification of neural networks focus on classification robustness (i.e., given an input x→0\vec{x}_{0} and true label yy, classification robustness requires ∀x→∈𝔹⁡(x→0,ϵ).arg​maxi⁡f​(x→)=y\forall\vec{x}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x}_{0};\epsilon)\ldotp\argmax_{i}f(\vec{x})=y).

So-called differentiable logics have been proposed to generate additional loss functions from arbitrary logical constraints, not limited to improving prediction accuracy. This additional loss term calculates a penalty depending on how much the network deviates from satisfying the constraint. Popular choices for differentiable logics include both systems designed specifically for use in neural networks, such as Deep Learning with Differentiable Logics (DL2) [22], as well as already existing and well-studied logical systems such as fuzzy logics.

The first in-depth study investigating the use of fuzzy logics as loss functions (called Differentiable Fuzzy Logics) was provided by [57] and presented insights into the learning characteristics of differentiable logic operators. A unifying framework of differentiable logics including DL2, fuzzy logics, and Signal Temporal Logic (STL), called Logic of Differentiable Logics (LDL), is provided in [52] and allows for mechanised proofs of theoretical properties of differentiable logics [1].

There are many differentiable logics to choose from, and these differ not only in terms of their domains and operators (compare ), but also when it comes to satisfying properties such as soundness, compositionality, smoothness, and shadow-lifting (which requires the truth value of a conjunction to increase whenever the truth value of one of its conjuncts increases). It has been shown [1, 59] that no differentiable logic can satisfy all desirable properties.

Flinkow et al. [23] have recently introduced a general differentiable logic library that implemented all major known differentiable logics under the same umbrella, allowing for their empirical comparative evaluation for the first time. Therein, it is assumed that all constraints are of the form ∀x→′∈𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ).ϕ\forall\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon)\ldotp\phi, i.e. a logical constraint should not only hold for a specific input x→\vec{x}, but also in its close vicinity. Therefore, the optimisation objective for the constraint ϕ\phi is shown in Eq. 5:

θ∗=arg​minθ⁡𝔼(x→,y→)∼𝒟​[λ​ℒ​(x→,y→,fθ)+(1−λ)​maxx→′∈𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ)​⟦ϕ⟧​(x→,x→′,y→,fθ)].\theta^{*}=\argmin\limits_{\theta}\expected\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\ \biggl[\lambda\mathcal{L}(\vec{x},\vec{y};f_{\theta})+(1-\lambda)\max\limits_{\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon)}\llbracket\phi\rrbracket_{\text{}}(\vec{x},\vec{x}^{\prime},\vec{y};f_{\theta})\biggr]. (5)

Here, ℒ\mathcal{L} denotes the prediction loss (e.g. cross-entropy loss ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} for classification, mean-squared-error loss ℒMSE\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} for regression, etc.), (x→,y→)∼𝒟(\vec{x},\vec{y})\sim\mathcal{D} is a pair of training data x→\vec{x} and target y→\vec{y} (i.e. the true label for classification, or the target value for regression), and λ\lambda is a hyperparameter required to balance the different loss terms.

In this paper, we will extend that library to cover the general properties ∀x→.𝒫⁡(x→)⟶𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})), as described in the introduction. At the same time, we inherit the functionality of compiling 𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})) to arbitrary DLs.

3 Combining Input Region Specification and Logical Constraint-based Loss

3.1 Definition of the Novel Optimisation Objective

We now introduce our generalised method formally. Given:

  • •

    a neural network fθ:ℝm→ℝnf_{\theta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} parametrised by training parameters θ\theta (such as neural network weights), and

  • •

    a constraint ϕ:∀x→∈ℝm.𝒫⁡(x→)⟶𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\phi\colon\forall\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\ldotp\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})) which we want to incorporate into optimisation for θ\theta,

we define a translation function ⦇⋅⦈\llparenthesis\cdot\rrparenthesis from a precondition 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) into a hyper-rectangle as follows. Assume 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) is given by an arbitrary Boolean formula containing atomic propositions only of the form li≤xi≤uil_{i}\leq x_{i}\leq u_{i}, for constants lil_{i}, uiu_{i}, and x→=[x1,…,xm]∈ℝm\vec{x}=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is a list of variables that denotes an input vector. Let l→min\vec{l}^{\text{min}} and u→max\vec{u}^{\text{max}} be constant vectors that define minimum lower and maximum upper bounds of x→\vec{x}33 3 In neural network verification, we always assume default lower and upper bounds are present (inferred from data) when some element vectors are not explicitly constrained. Examples in the rest of the paper illustrate that point..

If 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) is not satisfiable, we define ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈=∅\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis=\emptyset. Otherwise, we define ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis by induction on the structure of 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}):

  • •

    If 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) is of the form li≤xi≤uil_{i}\leq x_{i}\leq u_{i}, we form a hyper-rectangle H⁡(l→∗,u→∗)H(\vec{l}^{*},\vec{u}^{*}), where l→∗=l→min\vec{l}^{*}=\vec{l}^{\text{min}} except for its iith component being lil_{i} (and similarly obtain u→∗\vec{u}^{*}), and define ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈=H⁡(l→∗,u→∗)\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis=H(\vec{l}^{*},\vec{u}^{*}).

  • •

    If 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) is of the form ¬F\lnot F, where FF is an arbitrary formula, then ⦇F⦈=⦇F⦈∼\llparenthesis F\rrparenthesis=\llparenthesis F\rrparenthesis^{\sim};

  • •

    If 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) is of the form F1∨F2F_{1}\vee F_{2}, where F1,F2F_{1},F_{2} are arbitrary formulas, then ⦇F1∨F2⦈=⦇F1⦈∪⦇F2⦈\llparenthesis F_{1}\vee F_{2}\rrparenthesis=\llparenthesis F_{1}\rrparenthesis\cup\llparenthesis F_{2}\rrparenthesis;

  • •

    Lastly, if 𝒫⁡(x→)\mathcal{P}(\vec{x}) is of the form F1∧F2F_{1}\wedge F_{2}, then ⦇F1∨F2⦈=⦇F1⦈∩⦇F2⦈\llparenthesis F_{1}\vee F_{2}\rrparenthesis=\llparenthesis F_{1}\rrparenthesis\cap\llparenthesis F_{2}\rrparenthesis,

where ∼,∪,∩{}^{\sim},\cup,\cap stand for set-theoretic complement, union and intersection, respectively.

Recall that, by the construction of the previous section, we next define a translation function ⟦⋅⟧\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_{\text{}} from the postcondition 𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})) into real-valued loss, thus ⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{}} is defined.

Then, the optimisation objective for the constraint ϕ\phi is given as follows:

θ∗=arg​minθ⁡𝔼(x→,y→)∼𝒟​[λ​ℒ​(x→,y→,fθ)+(1−λ)​maxx→′∈⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈​⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧​(x→,x→′,y→,fθ)].\theta^{*}=\argmin\limits_{\theta}\expected\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\ \biggl[\lambda\mathcal{L}(\vec{x},\vec{y};f_{\theta})+(1-\lambda)\max\limits_{\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis}\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{}}(\vec{x},\vec{x}^{\prime},\vec{y};f_{\theta})\biggr]. (6)

Note the similarity to the optimisation objective previously shown in Eq. 5. However, to find adversarial examples for the constraint loss, the inner maximisation problem maxx→′∈⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈⁡⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧​(x→,x→′,y→,fθ)\max_{\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis}\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{}}(\vec{x},\vec{x}^{\prime},\vec{y};f_{\theta}) is approximated using a modified PGD attack that works with arbitrary hyper-rectangles given by ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis.

3.2 Examples from the Literature in Our Terms

We briefly show how well-studied properties from the literature can be seen as sub-cases of the unified approach we proposed in this section.

ACAS Xu.

The ACAS Xu neural networks take six sensor measurements as inputs and produce scores for five possible advisories, “clear-of-conflict” (COC), “weak left” (WL), “weak right” (WR), “strong left” (SL), or “strong right” (SR).

As a representative example, we take property ϕ2\phi_{2} from [30], which requires that the score for a “clear of conflict” advisory should never be maximal for a distant, significantly slower intruder, meaning that it can never be the worst action to take.

  • •

    Obtaining ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis: The intruder being distant and significantly slower translates to the following lower bounds on network inputs:

    55 947.691 ft≤ρ,1145 ft/s≤vown,vintruder≤60 ft/s,$55\,947.691\text{\,}\mathrm{ft}$\leq\rho,\quad$1145\text{\,}\mathrm{ft}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$\leq v_{\text{own}},\quad v_{\text{intruder}}\leq$60\text{\,}\mathrm{ft}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$, (7)

    which directly give rise to a hyper-rectangle: assuming the inputs to the network to be a vector x→=[ρ,θ,ψ,vown,vintruder]\vec{x}=[\rho,\theta,\psi,v_{\text{own}},v_{\text{intruder}}], the hyper-rectangle induced by Eq. 7 translates to lower bound l→\vec{l} and upper bound u→\vec{u} as

    l→=max⁡{l→min,[55 947.691 ft,−∞,−∞,1145 ft/s,60 ft/s]},and​u→=u→max,\vec{l}=\max\{\vec{l}^{\text{min}},[$55\,947.691\text{\,}\mathrm{ft}$,-\infty,-\infty,$1145\text{\,}\mathrm{ft}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$,$60\text{\,}\mathrm{ft}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$]\},\ \text{and}\ \vec{u}=\vec{u}^{\text{max}}, (8)

    where l→min\vec{l}^{\text{min}} and u→max\vec{u}^{\text{max}} denote the minimum and maximum permitted values for each of the six parameters, and max⁡{⋅,⋅}\max\{\cdot,\cdot\} is applied component-wise.

  • •

    Obtaining ⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{}}: The constraint on the output, i.e. the score for a “clear of conflict” advisory should never be maximal, can be expressed as the disjunction

    (yCOC<yWL)∨(yCOC<yWR)∨(yCOC<ySL)∨(yCOC<ySR),(y_{\text{COC}}<y_{\text{WL}})\vee(y_{\text{COC}}<y_{\text{WR}})\vee(y_{\text{COC}}<y_{\text{SL}})\vee(y_{\text{COC}}<y_{\text{SR}}), (9)

    and translated into loss using the mappings ⟦t<t′⟧\llbracket t<t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{}} and ⟦t∨t′⟧\llbracket t\vee t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{}} of a chosen differentiable logic. The actual translation is omitted here for the sake of brevity, but can be obtained by repeated application of ⟦t∨t′⟧\llbracket t\vee t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{}} and the identity ⟦t<t′⟧=⟦t≤t′∧t≠t′⟧\llbracket t<t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{}}=\llbracket t\leq t^{\prime}\wedge t\neq t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{}}.

Standard robustness.

A property that is often of interest for image classification problems is standard robustness [11], expressed as

∀x→′∈𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ).∥f⁡(x→)−f⁡(x→′)∥≤δ.\forall\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon)\ldotp\lVert f(\vec{x})-f(\vec{x}^{\prime})\rVert\leq\delta. (10)

This property states that there is a maximum allowed distance the output may be perturbed for a slightly perturbed input (while not making any requirements about correctly classifying either input or perturbed input, which fits the general notion of robustness).

  • •

    Obtaining ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis: In this case, the input region specification is obtained by combining the ϵ\epsilon-cubes around each image x→i\vec{x}_{i} in the training set {(x→i,y→i)}i=1n\{(\vec{x}_{i},\vec{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} and filtering on only valid images44 4 Without loss of generality, assume that pixels can take a value between 00 and 11, and thus valid images made up of mm pixels are in the set [0,1]m[0,1]^{m}., thus we obtain

    ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈=[0,1]m∩𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ).\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis=[0,1]^{m}\cap\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon). (11)
  • •

    Obtaining ⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{}}: The output constraint is obtained using the mapping ⟦t≤t′⟧\llbracket t\leq t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{}} of a chosen differentiable logic. For example, using DL2’s mapping ⟦t≤t′⟧DL2=max{0,t−t′}\llbracket t\leq t^{\prime}\rrbracket_{\text{DL2}}=\max\{0,t-t^{\prime}\}, the resulting loss function would be

    ⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧DL2=max⁡{0,∥f⁡(x→′)−f⁡(x→)∥−δ}.\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{DL2}}=\max\{0,\lVert f(\vec{x}^{\prime})-f(\vec{x})\rVert-\delta\}. (12)

3.3 Implementation

We briefly describe our PyTorch [48] implementation of this training framework, publicly available at https://github.com/tflinkow/property-driven-ml. Our main aim is to provide a generic, reusable framework that is easy to use and easy to adapt to new scenarios, while at the same time computationally efficient enough to be useful.

Hyper-rectangles are internally stored as lower and upper bounds of the same shape as the data, allowing for efficient operations (such as sampling and projection) for PGD. For convenience, shortcuts such as EpsilonBall(eps: float) are implemented, which automatically create upper and lower bounds for each data point in the dataset. Our implementation makes these hyper-rectangles part of the dataset; by extending torch.utils.data.Dataset, the corresponding hyper-rectangles can easily be obtained with the training data and labels. Figure 2 shows how to create and use ϵ\epsilon-balls for MNIST during training.

On the loss function side, we aim to achieve an easy-to-use framework by taking a parametric approach for expressing logical constraints: logical operations on an abstract Logic object that provides common operations such as LEQ, AND, OR, IMPLIES, etc., allow the user to specify logical constraints without having to make the choice of differentiable logic (or to even be aware of differences in their operators or domains), as can be seen in Fig. 3.

Lastly, we provide two important enhancements that reduce the number of hyperparameters the user has to tune, while at the same time achieving higher effectiveness of the training process: (1) balancing the two loss terms is handled by the adaptive loss-balancing algorithm GradNorm [13], and (2) a modified implementation of AutoPGD [14], for achieving better results than standard PGD, whose effectiveness has been shown to strongly rely on good attack parameters [46, 15].

4 Experimental Set-up & Results

All experiments ran on Google Colab; the MNIST experiment described in Section 4.1 ran on an A100 GPU instance with 40 GB40\text{\,}\mathrm{GB} of VRAM, and the drone controller case study described in Section 4.2 ran on a v5e-1 TPU with 47 GB47\text{\,}\mathrm{GB} of RAM. All experiments ran for 100100 epochs and utilised the AdamW [41] optimiser with learning rate 1×10−31\text{\times}{10}^{-3} and weight decay of 1×10−41\text{\times}{10}^{-4}. The MNIST experiment described in Section 4.1, used 2020 PGD iterations and 3030 random restarts; the drone controller experiment described in Section 4.2, used 5050 PGD iterations and 8080 random restarts. Running all experiments took 1 d1\text{\,}\mathrm{d} 2 h2\text{\,}\mathrm{h} 38 min38\text{\,}\mathrm{min} to complete.

Evaluation metrics.

For each logical property ϕ:𝒫⁡(x→)⟶𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\phi\colon\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})), we report results for training without any logical loss translation (called baseline), as well as for training with the DL2 and fuzzy logic differentiable losses. All experimental results are obtained by measuring the network’s performance on the test set 𝒯={(x→i,y→i)}i=1n\mathcal{T}=\{(\vec{x}_{i},\vec{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} using various metrics we will define in the following. The test set consists of pairs of input data x→i\vec{x}_{i} and target data y→i\vec{y}_{i} (i.e. the true label for classification, or the target value for regression). Further, let [P][P] denote the Iverson bracket, returning 11 if PP is true, and 00 otherwise, and let ⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧BL\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{BL}} denote its standard Boolean logic interpretation, used to evaluate whether the constraint is satisfied or not.

In order to evaluate the network’s prediction performance, for classification problems we report the network’s Prediction Accuracy (PAcc), defined as the fraction of correct predictions:

PAcc:=1|𝒯|∑(x→,y→)∈𝒯[f(x→)=y→],\text{PAcc}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\in\mathcal{T}}[f(\vec{x})=\vec{y}], (13)

whereas for regression problems, we make use of the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) metric, defined as the average difference between the network’s predictions and the target values:

RMSE:=1|𝒯|​∑(x→,y→)∈𝒯(f⁡(x→)−y→)2.\text{RMSE}:=\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\in\mathcal{T}}(f(\vec{x})-\vec{y})^{2}}. (14)

Additionally, in order to quantify how well a network satisfies a logical constraint ϕ\phi, we define two additional evaluation metrics, first proposed in [11]. We define Constraint Accuracy (CAcc) as the fraction of random samples x→rnd\vec{x}_{\text{rnd}} that satisfy constraint ϕ\phi:

CAcc:=1|𝒯|​∑(x→,y→)∈𝒯[⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧BL​(x→,x→rnd,y→)],\text{CAcc}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\in\mathcal{T}}[\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{BL}}(\vec{x};\vec{x}_{\text{rnd}};\vec{y})], (15)

where, for each (x→,y→)∈𝒯(\vec{x},\vec{y})\in\mathcal{T}, a fresh random sample x→rnd\vec{x}_{\text{rnd}} is drawn from ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis.

In addition to that, let Constraint Security (CSec) be the fraction of adversarial samples x→adv\vec{x}_{\text{adv}} within that satisfy constraint ϕ\phi:

CSec:=1|𝒯|​∑(x→,y→)∈𝒯[⟦𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))⟧BL​(x→,x→adv,y→)],\text{CSec}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\vec{x},\vec{y})\in\mathcal{T}}[\llbracket\mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x}))\rrbracket_{\text{BL}}(\vec{x};\vec{x}_{\text{adv}};\vec{y})], (16)

where, for each (x→,y→)∈𝒯(\vec{x},\vec{y})\in\mathcal{T}, a fresh adversarial sample x→adv\vec{x}_{\text{adv}} within ⦇𝒫⁡(x→)⦈\llparenthesis\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\rrparenthesis is obtained using PGD.

4.1 Case Study: MNIST

In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a well-known machine learning example, we will train a simple convolutional neural network with ReLU activations to satisfy the standard robustness [11] constraint shown in Eq. 17 on the MNIST [37] data set.

∀x→′∈𝔹⁡(x→,ϵ).∥f⁡(x→)−f⁡(x→′)∥∞≤δ\forall\vec{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}(\vec{x};\epsilon)\ldotp\ \lVert f(\vec{x})-f(\vec{x}^{\prime})\rVert_{\infty}\leq\delta (17)

Here, the hyper-rectangles that specify the relevant input regions are obtained as the ϵ\epsilon-cubes around all inputs in the train set. We chose ϵ=0.3\epsilon=0.3 and δ=0.05\delta=0.05.

The results are shown in Figs. 4 and 1 and report prediction accuracy (PAcc), constraint satisfaction on random samples (CAcc), and on adversarial samples (CSec), as defined in Eqs. 13, 15 and 16. To avoid prioritising one metric over another, we consider the best result to be the one that maximises their product. Table 1 reports the best epoch of the last 1010 epochs, which is also marked in Fig. 4. It can be seen that property-driven training leads to significantly improved constraint satisfaction at the expense of prediction accuracy.

4.2 Case Study: Neural Network Drone Controller

Because the training data for ACAS Xu is not released, we instead consider a neural network controller with similar characteristics as a more sophisticated case study. Our case study, proposed in [33], revolves around a neural network controller for a gliding drone inspired by the flying seeds of Alsomitra macrocarpa, the Javan cucumber, shown in Fig. 5(a). These flying seeds are capable of stable flight over long distances due to their unique shape [12].

The aim of the neural network controller is for the gliding drone to follow a desired trajectory in two-dimensional space (shown in Fig. 5(b)). The path of the drone is simulated with a two-dimensional aerodynamic model for falling plates with displaced centre of mass [38], whereby the controller actuates the position of the centre of mass to alter the drone trajectory. The neural network controller takes as input the six parameters of the dynamic system shown in Table 2 and outputs a value (the displacement of the position of the centre of mass) that can range from 0.181 to 0.1930.1810.193. The equation for the desired trajectory is y=−xy=-x.

We use a small three-layer feedforward neural network with hidden layers of sizes 6464 and 3232, respectively. Each layer is followed by a ReLU activation.

Desired properties.

In general, we want the drone to follow the trajectory as closely as possible; more specifically, we want it to satisfy the properties defined formally in Eqs. 18, 19, 20 and 21 below. Note that each property is defined locally for an input x→0\vec{x}_{0}.

  1. 1.

    If the drone is far above the line, the neural network output will always make the drone pitch down:

    ϕ1​(x→0):∀x→.𝖿𝖺𝗋𝖠𝖻𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(x→0,x→)⟶f⁡(x→)≥0.187.\phi_{1}(\vec{x}_{0})\colon\quad\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\ \mathsf{farAboveLine}(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ f(\vec{x})\geq 0.187. (18)
  2. 2.

    If the drone is close to the line and at an appropriate pitch angle, the neural network output will be intermediate:

    ϕ2(x→0):∀x→.𝖼𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗈𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(x→0,x→)∧𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗉𝗋𝗂𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖯𝗂𝗍𝖼𝗁𝖠𝗇𝗀𝗅𝖾⁡(x→)⟶ 0.184≤f⁡(x→′)≤0.19.\begin{split}\phi_{2}(\vec{x}_{0})\colon\quad\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\ &\mathsf{closeToLine}(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x})\\ \wedge\ &\mathsf{appropriatePitchAngle}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ 0.184\leq f(\vec{x}^{\prime})\leq 0.19.\end{split} (19)
  3. 3.

    If the drone is above and close to the line, pitching down quickly and moving fast, the neural network output will always make the drone pitch up:

    ϕ3(x→0):∀x→.𝖺𝖻𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖠𝗇𝖽𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗈𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(x→0,x→)∧𝗉𝗂𝗍𝖼𝗁𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖣𝗈𝗐𝗇𝖰𝗎𝗂𝖼𝗄𝗅𝗒⁡(x→)∧𝗆𝗈𝗏𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖥𝖺𝗌𝗍⁡(x→)⟶f⁡(x→)≤0.187.\begin{split}\phi_{3}(\vec{x}_{0})\colon\quad\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\ &\mathsf{aboveAndCloseToLine}(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x})\\ \wedge\ &\mathsf{pitchingDownQuickly}(\vec{x})\\ \wedge\ &\mathsf{movingFast}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ f(\vec{x})\leq 0.187.\end{split} (20)
  4. 4.

    Lastly, as neural networks with ReLU activations are Lipschitz-continuous [53], and Lipschitz robustness is the strongest form of robustness [11], we are particularly interested for the network to satisfy the property:

    ϕ4​(x→0):∀x→.𝖼𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗈𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(𝗑→𝟢,𝗑→)⟶∥f⁡(x→0)−f⁡(x→)∥2≤L​∥x→0−x→∥2.\phi_{4}(\vec{x}_{0})\colon\quad\forall\vec{x}\ldotp\ \mathsf{closeToLine(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x})}\ \longrightarrow\ \lVert f(\vec{x}_{0})-f(\vec{x})\rVert_{2}\leq L\lVert\vec{x}_{0}-\vec{x}\rVert_{2}. (21)

    Note that a smaller value of LL means a smoother output, and therefore a more robust network. We use a value of L=0.3L=0.3 in our experiment.

In the above property definitions, we make use of the predicates below to present the desired properties as clearly as possible. First, let x→=[vx′,vy′,ω,θ,x,y]\vec{x}=[v_{x^{\prime}},v_{y^{\prime}},\omega,\theta,x,y] denote an input vector consisting of the six system parameters. We then use ω(x→)\omega^{(\vec{x})} to refer to the ω\omega component of x→\vec{x} (similarly for its other components). Then, the predicates are defined as shown below:

𝖿𝖺𝗋𝖠𝖻𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(x→0,x→)\displaystyle\mathsf{farAboveLine}(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x}) :=y(x→)≥2−x(x→0)\displaystyle:=\quad y^{(\vec{x})}\geq 2-x^{(\vec{x}_{0})} (22)
𝖼𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗈𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(x→0,x→)\displaystyle\mathsf{closeToLine}(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x}) :=−2−x(x→0)≤y(x→)≤2−x(x→0)\displaystyle:=\quad-2-x^{(\vec{x}_{0})}\leq y^{(\vec{x})}\leq 2-x^{(\vec{x}_{0})} (23)
𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗉𝗋𝗂𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖯𝗂𝗍𝖼𝗁𝖠𝗇𝗀𝗅𝖾⁡(x→)\displaystyle\mathsf{appropriatePitchAngle}(\vec{x}) :=−0.786≤θ(x→)≤−0.747\displaystyle:=\quad-0.786\leq\theta^{(\vec{x})}\leq-0.747 (24)
𝖺𝖻𝗈𝗏𝖾𝖠𝗇𝖽𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗈𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖾⁡(x→0,x→)\displaystyle\mathsf{aboveAndCloseToLine}(\vec{x}_{0},\vec{x}) :=−x(x→0)≤y(x→)≤2−x(x→0)\displaystyle:=\quad-x^{(\vec{x}_{0})}\leq y^{(\vec{x})}\leq 2-x^{(\vec{x}_{0})} (25)
𝗉𝗂𝗍𝖼𝗁𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖣𝗈𝗐𝗇𝖰𝗎𝗂𝖼𝗄𝗅𝗒⁡(x→)\displaystyle\mathsf{pitchingDownQuickly}(\vec{x}) :=ω(x→)≤−0.12\displaystyle:=\quad\omega^{(\vec{x})}\leq-0.12 (26)
𝗆𝗈𝗏𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖥𝖺𝗌𝗍⁡(x→)\displaystyle\mathsf{movingFast}(\vec{x}) :=vx′(x→)≤−0.3\displaystyle:=\quad v_{x^{\prime}}^{(\vec{x})}\leq-0.3 (27)

The results of training networks to satisfy the desired properties are shown in Table 3 and confirm that property-driven training leads to considerably improved constraint satisfaction. Again, we note that this increase in constraint satisfaction comes at the expense of regression performance, visualised in Fig. 6.

5 Discussion

We have described a generalised framework for property-driven machine learning and evaluated an implementation on two case studies; a classification example in Section 4.1, and a regression example in Section 4.2. In both cases, constraint satisfaction could be significantly improved for models obtained via property-driven training compared to models trained in a standard manner, however at the expense of prediction performance (a known result, compare e.g. [55]).

5.1 Related Work

Some of the ideas presented in this paper were already suggested by Fischer et al. [22]. However, while they mention arbitrary box constraints (i.e. hyper-rectangles), they do not provide a motivation of why those might prove to be useful in certain use cases, and their evaluation utilises only ϵ\epsilon-balls.

ULLER [58] is a language for neuro-symbolic AI that allows for fuzzy, classical, and probabilistic semantics. An implementation does not yet exist and is mentioned as future work.

PYLON [2] is a Python framework for property-driven training, however, constraints are limited to constraints on the outputs of the model, without employing PGD or other methods to find adversarial examples that violate the constraints.

Lastly, Giunchiglia et al. [25] provide a survey of property-driven machine learning, including specialised neural network architectures and other approaches to obtain hard guarantees of constraint satisfaction.

5.2 Conclusion

This work can be seen as a stepping stone towards a more general compilation procedure from logical properties to optimisation objectives, announced as a target of the language Vehicle [19, 17, 16, 20, 18]. However, we note that at the time of submitting the paper, Vehicle’s algorithm is not yet finalised; and thus we cannot make a technical comparison with the results presented here.

Limitations and future work.

While they are computationally effective, hyper-rectangles are not the most precise geometric representation of an input region. For example, the properties for the Alsomitra drone controller as originally proposed in [33] involve bounds on components of the input vector that depend on its other components, e.g. in ϕ1:∀x→.y(x→)≥2−x(x→)\phi_{1}\colon\quad\forall\vec{x}\ldotp y^{(\vec{x})}\geq 2-x^{(\vec{x})}, the bounds on the yy-component of the input vector x→\vec{x} depend on the value of its own xx-component. These bounds give rise to a half-space, and they cannot be represented as a hyper-rectangle that requires constant lower and upper bounds for each dimension. Casadio et al. [10] note that a convex hull would capture input regions the most accurately, however, constructing this would be computationally expensive.

On the other hand, loss-based methods provide (almost) no guarantees, as confirmed in [23]. It will be a worthwhile future research direction to investigate whether certified training [61, 62, 45, 49] methods can be integrated into this framework.

An interesting subject for further study is to define in more precise terms the fragment of FOL that can covered by the admissible verification properties that correspond to optimisation objectives. The property ∀x→∈ℝm.𝒫⁡(x→)⟶𝒬⁡(f⁡(x→))\forall\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\ldotp\mathcal{P}(\vec{x})\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}(f(\vec{x})) clearly has a clausal form, and there is a long history of studying first-order Horn clauses and first-order hereditary Harrop clauses as optimal fragments of FOL for automated reasoning and verification [44, 5].

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
